name: Battle of Jena–Auerstedt
info: On 14 October 1806 Napoleon's army defeated Prince Hohenlohe's Prussians at Jena while Marshal Davout's single corps beat the main Prussian army at Auerstedt, in the War of the Fourth Coalition; Prussia's resistance collapsed in the weeks after.

facts.date: Tuesday 14 October 1806, two battles fought on the same day
facts.place: Near Jena and Auerstedt, then in the Duchy of Saxe-Weimar and the Kingdom of Prussia, now in Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, Germany
facts.sides: At Jena, the French under Napoleon I (initially 48,000, rising to 96,000 in the area, of whom 40,000 fought) against a Prussian army under Prince Hohenlohe. At Auerstedt, Marshal Davout's III Corps against the main Prussian army of 64,000 under the Duke of Brunswick and King Frederick William III. Before the campaign the Prussians and Saxons together numbered about 130,000 Prussians and 20,000 Saxons against a French force of 180,000.
facts.outcome: The French won both battles. Prussian losses were 10,000 killed or wounded and 15,000 prisoners at Jena, and 13,000 casualties at Auerstedt against 7,052 for Davout's corps.

t: Two battles were fought on 14 October 1806: Napoleon thought he was facing the main Prussian army at Jena, but it was Davout's III Corps at Auerstedt that met it, outnumbered more than two to one.

The Prussian command was divided between several officers, had no quick courier system and lost the initiative to Napoleon before the fighting began; both the Duke of Brunswick and Schmettau were mortally or badly wounded at Auerstedt.

Within weeks most of the Prussian army had been captured, and the defeat led reformers who had served at the battle, among them Scharnhorst, Gneisenau and Clausewitz, to begin remaking the Prussian state.
dyk: Napoleon at first refused to believe that Davout's single corps had beaten the Prussian main body, and answered the first report with "Your Marshal must be seeing double!", a reference to Davout's poor eyesight.
ev: Prussia declares war and Napoleon sends 180,000 men through the Franconian Forest towards Saxony and Berlin
Napoleon defeats Hohenlohe's Prussians near Jena
Davout's III Corps defeats the main Prussian army at Auerstedt, where the Duke of Brunswick is mortally wounded
A large body of Prussian troops surrenders in the Capitulation of Erfurt
Davout leads his III Corps into Berlin
Hohenlohe's force surrenders after the Battle of Prenzlau
Blücher's corps is surrounded at Lübeck and surrenders the next day
The siege of Magdeburg ends with Ney's capture of the fortress

sections.background:
The two battles were fought in the War of the Fourth Coalition. Prussia had begun its mobilisation almost a month before France, but Napoleon had kept a high state of readiness since the Russian refusal to accept defeat in the War of the Third Coalition. He planned to force Prussia into a decisive battle, like Austerlitz, and to pre-empt a Prussian offensive. A major part of the Grande Armée stood in what is now Baden-Württemberg in south-west Germany, and he decided on an advance north-east into Saxony and on to Berlin.

After the Prussian declaration of war Napoleon thrust a force of 180,000 through the Franconian Forest. The Prussian army awaited him with about 130,000 Prussians and 20,000 Saxons. Its command was bloated and inefficient. Key roles were divided between several officers, and the post of chief of staff was held by three, General Phull, Colonel Gerhard von Scharnhorst and Colonel Rudolf Massenbach. The confusion caused a delay of over a month before the final order of battle was prepared, and five main plans were argued over, so that the initiative passed to the French and the Prussian plans became reactions to Napoleon's movements.

There was no courier system to carry messages quickly, and a changed order cost precious minutes. Prussian doctrines had stood unchanged for more than 50 years, while the French army had been reorganised on the corps system, which Napoleon had greatly improved by 1805.
sections.forces:
On the French side Napoleon commanded in person at Jena, while at Auerstedt the French force was a single corps, Marshal Louis-Nicolas Davout's III Corps. Napoleon's force at Jena was initially 48,000 strong, and by his carefully planned and flexible dispositions he reached local superiority with a force of 96,000 men. Less than half of them fought the Prussians, since only 40,000 were sent and actually took part. He kept the Imperial Guard under his direct command. Marshal Bernadotte's I Corps was elsewhere, ordered towards Dornburg.

The Prussian and Saxon army was divided into three armies drawn from across Prussia. At Jena the commander was Prince Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, and Rüchel was to bring 15,000 men from Weimar. At Auerstedt the main Prussian army of 64,000 men included King Frederick William III, the Duke of Brunswick as overall commander, and Field Marshals von Möllendorf and von Kalckreuth. Friedrich Wilhelm von Schmettau led a division and Blücher the cavalry. The Prussian cavalry was better than the French and its infantry formidable. The musket of 1806, the model of 1754, was called "the worst in Europe" by one authority, and many soldiers in the royal army were recruited non-Prussians.

Davout's III Corps, outnumbered at Auerstedt by more than two to one, was superbly trained and disciplined. His divisions were those of Étienne Gudin, Louis Friant and Morand.
sections.course:
The battle of Jena began on the morning of 14 October. The French first attacked both flanks of the Prussian line while the supporting troops took position. The French general Saint-Hilaire broke through and isolated the Prussian left flank. Marshal Ney attacked without orders. His first assault succeeded, but he was overextended and under heavy artillery fire, and a Prussian counterattack enveloped him; he formed his men into a square. Napoleon ordered Marshal Lannes to shift from the centre to help Ney and put the Imperial Guard in the weakened centre. Ney was rescued, and the Prussian commanders did not press the French weakness. Around 1 p.m. Napoleon ordered his flanks to push hard and encircle the Prussian centre. The flank attacks succeeded and the Prussians withdrew.

At Auerstedt Gudin's division was on the move from Naumburg before 6:30 a.m. and was stopped outside Poppel by Prussian cavalry and artillery. Davout ordered Gudin to deploy at Hassenhausen. Schmettau and Blücher pushed Gudin back to the village. Friant's division and the 12-pound artillery arrived at 9:30 a.m., and the French formed squares. Davout hid his chasseurs à cheval behind a hill and used them against Blücher's cavalry, three of whose regiments were routed. Shortly before 10 a.m. Brunswick ordered a full assault on Hassenhausen, but by 10 a.m. he was carried off mortally wounded, along with the badly wounded Schmettau, and the Prussian command broke down. Davout counter-attacked at 11 a.m. By noon Schmettau's centre had been forced back over the Lissbach Stream and the King ordered a withdrawal.
sections.aftermath:
At Jena the Prussian army lost 10,000 killed or wounded, 15,000 prisoners and 150 guns; the French lost 5,000 killed, wounded or captured. At Auerstedt Davout's corps lost 7,052 officers and men killed or wounded, against Prussian casualties of 13,000. Napoleon at first doubted that one corps had beaten the Prussian main body. Davout was made Duke of Auerstedt and was given the honour of entering Berlin first, which he did on 25 October with his exhausted III Corps. Lannes, the hero of Jena, was not so honoured.

Murat's cavalry pursued the Prussians relentlessly. A large body of troops became prisoners in the Capitulation of Erfurt on 16 October with hardly a shot fired, and Bernadotte defeated the Duke of Württemberg's Prussian Reserve Army at Halle on 17 October. Hohenlohe surrendered on 28 October after the Battle of Prenzlau, followed by the Capitulation of Pasewalk. Blücher, with 21,000 men at large west of the Oder, was pursued by the French and blocked from Denmark, and his corps and Winning's was surrounded at Lübeck on 6 and 7 November. The Prussians lost 3,000 killed and wounded there, and Blücher surrendered with 9,000 other prisoners. The siege of Magdeburg ended on 11 November.

Bernadotte's inaction at Auerstedt became controversial within a week. He and Davout later became bitter enemies, and Napoleon sent him a severely worded reprimand but took no further action.
sections.sources:
Napoleon believed after the fighting that he had faced the main Prussian army at Jena, and so doubted Davout's first reports. The strengths on the French side are disputed ground: at Jena 48,000 grew to 96,000 in the area with 40,000 engaged, and at Auerstedt Davout is said only to have been outnumbered more than two to one. The battle is also known through later commentators such as Nikolai Orlov, who praised Davout's choice of Mount Eckartsberga as his main effort, and Martin van Creveld, who judged Napoleon's command at Jena.

What is most disputed is Bernadotte. Davout received a courier from Berthier before dawn on 14 October saying that the Prince of Ponte Corvo might march with him, but that the Emperor hoped he would be at Dornburg, and Davout passed the order on at 4 a.m. Napoleon said on St Helena that Bernadotte's conduct was disgraceful. Contemporary evidence shows no recriminations that night, and a later search of the orders and dispatches found no order for Bernadotte to march with Davout. Colonel Ernst Marsh Lloyd suggested that Napoleon was shifting blame for Davout having to fight alone.
sections.legacy:
The battles showed the need to reform a very feudal Prussian state and army. Scharnhorst, Gneisenau and Clausewitz, who served in them, along with Blücher and Boyen, took part in the reforms that, together with civilian reforms of the following years, began Prussia's transformation into a modern state. That modernised Prussia took the lead in expelling France from Germany. The reduction of Prussia to a French vassal and the revolt that restored its national honour formed a key component of German nationalism.

Martin van Creveld wrote that Napoleon at Jena had known nothing of the main action of the day, forgotten two of his corps and had one of his principal subordinates disobey in a way that would have brought a lesser man before a firing squad, yet won what was probably the great single triumph of his career.

Napoleon named a bridge in Paris after the battle, and after his defeat the Prussian contingent of the occupation forces wished to destroy it until Talleyrand temporarily renamed it. The Paris Metro station keeps the name. Near Jena hiking trails are named after Napoleon and his marshals and a museum at Cospeda tells of the battle. It was re-enacted on 14 October 2006 with 1,800 participants, and the association Jena 1806 e. V. holds commemorative events each October.

summary: On 14 October 1806 Napoleon defeated Hohenlohe's Prussians at Jena while Davout's single corps beat the main Prussian army at Auerstedt. The Prussian army was largely captured within weeks, and the defeat prompted the reforms of Scharnhorst, Gneisenau and Clausewitz.
references: D. Plunket Barton, Bernadotte and Napoleon: 1763–1810 (John Murray, 1921)
notes: The lead says the Prussian force at Jena was under Hohenlohe and Napoleon commanded the French there; the Overview gives Hohenlohe's loss as 10,000 killed or wounded and 15,000 captured, matching the Battle section. The 150 guns appear only in the Battle section.

Strengths: Davout's own strength is not given; only 'outnumbered more than two to one' against the Prussian main force of 64,000. The 96,000 of Napoleon's force 'reaching' in the area against 40,000 engaged is as the article words it.
The article says Napoleon's praise for Davout and calls the victory 'glorious' in its own voice; praise left out. The 'decisive engagement' of the lead is not repeated as a verdict.
The sources section is thin: the article names few primary sources, so it turns to the Bernadotte dispute and later commentators. Napoleon's own St Helena claim is given as the article gives it.
The article spells Dornburg and Dornberg, Auerstedt and Auerstadt, Ruchel and Rüchel; I used Dornburg, Auerstedt, Rüchel. The 'Prince of Ponte Corvo' is Bernadotte in the quoted order.

Left out: the Advantage of terrain reference (no such section in the text), la maraude, the Davout quotation by Orlov beyond its main point, the 'Pursuit of the Three Marshals' detail, Boldekow, Anklam, Wolgast and Wismar captures, the film 'Into the Battle'.
'Bernadotte later cited ... verbal order' and 'the Prussians at Jena withdrew once they saw French troops occupying their line of retreat' left out for length.

Slight inconsistency: the Overview says Rüchel's men were ridden over after Hohenlohe's force was routed, with Rüchel wounded; the Battle section does not mention Rüchel's arrival. I mention only his 15,000.
